utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Three short matters. First, we have just received a revised copy of this witness summary. The original came in to us at about 8.00 last night. We would like to move in limine to preclude this witness from testifying about matters or events outside the period covered by the amended indictment, and I can, I think, alert the Court's attention to the particular paragraphs that we had in mind. The first is paragraph 37, the second is 38, the third is 39, and finally paragraphs 40 to 42, which were apparently added today. The second application that we would like to make is to limit this witness to testifying about facts rather than the expansive opinions that are contained in this offer of proof, the most significant and particular of which is paragraph 31, which analogises Mr. Kordic's position to that of Adolf Hitler, but also to the opinions contained in paragraphs 24, 27, 29, 30, and 35. And finally, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 27, 29, 30, and 33, in addition to paragraph 31. And the third and final point is that we do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be easier to deal with these points separately --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- rather than trying to run them together. The first point you take is that there is reference to matters at the end of the statement, paragraphs 37 onward --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- which deals with times outside the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And with the Court's permission, when matters of opinion come up as to which we object specifically, perhaps I could draw the Court's attention to that at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Looking first of all at paragraphs 37 onward, whether or not it's outside the date of the indictment, it doesn't seem to be terribly important and I wouldn't have thought very contentious evidence. What's really the objection to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, one example would be, Your Honour, paragraph 38 appears to be a hearsay statement made by someone other than the accused at a time outside of the amended indictment. And we have been provided with a copy of this witness's contemporaneous diary, or at least pieces of it; I did not see any such entry in the contemporaneous diary. Accordingly, we're not in a position to concede that matter at all, even if it were relevant, which I do not believe it to be. But the last point, Your Honour, is with respect to leading questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with this point. Let's finish this point. Ms. Somers, yes, what do you say about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, the fact that certain things that the witness knows came to him at a point outside the indictment is irrelevant. What is relevant is that this Court has an obligation under Rule 85(A), sub (vi), to have before it "any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty on" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- "one or more of the charges in the indictment," all of which must come in during the course of the trial. Further, the actual text refers to times within the time of the indictment. The fact that there are things that happened in '94 is a continuum of the political activities, or they concern personae who were very much at the heart of this indictment. So the relevance is direct, but clearly Rule 85 would require that the Court know what Dario Kordic was doing from the time of the indictment all the way through the time of apprehension, or surrender, as he calls it. On Point 38, if the Court reads the question, it talks about a comment made by Valenta, and it refers directly to the things that happened during the Muslim/Croat conflict, which is absolutely the heart of this indictment. Further, if the Defence wishes to cross-examine or to have Mr. Valenta testify, the Defence is free to so bring him. Virtually every point that has been raised by the Defence has no merit, and in fact, the information is critical to this Court's hearing a full picture of this defendant's activities and authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Sayers, could we not agree about the period covered by the indictment? It is of course quite clear that if a testimony goes beyond the period of the indictment, and in order to cause prejudice, and has nothing to do with other counts, that objection would perhaps stand. But here we are only dealing with some information which is relevant and which is relevant to various counts of the indictment and the period of the indictment, even if it refers to a period after the period covered by the indictment. But I believe that we are fully entitled to hear this information, that is, to establish the truth regarding the indictment itself. Therefore your objection really should tell us, is it that it deals with some facts which have nothing to do with the indictment, or rather that they would represent some additional charges? But the fact that it goes beyond the period covered by the indictment I do not think provides sufficient grounds to object to this testimony, unless it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. For the reasons Judge Bennouna has set out, we will admit the evidence. Your next point had to do with the various opinions which were --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- mentioned; yes. Perhaps you could deal with that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would be happy to. This witness is no different from any other witness who comes before the Court, and of course the witness should be permitted to talk about the facts of which he knows. But if he proceeds to give wide-ranging, tall political opinions of the type that are contained in the paragraphs that I've just recited to the Court, then unfortunately we have to consume time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which paragraph again? Remind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The one about Hitler?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Number 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then there were a variety of others, but paragraph 31 is the most representative. Obviously, the Court is concerned with expediency, for reasons we went into last week. If the witness is permitted to express all manner of opinions like this, we have to consume valuable time going into these matters. And the Court has pointed out on occasion, and perhaps appropriately, that obviously these matters are not really a memory contest, but really it is, in a sense, if the witness volunteers all manner of opinions on the subject and then is shown subsequently to lack a valid or sufficient factual foundation for the utterance of those opinions. So that's the basis for our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just dealing with it for a moment, and we can discuss it: The witness has had an extensive military career -- we can see this between paragraphs 1 to 15 -- he's had various jobs involving the analysis of political matters, so we can see that. Whatever the appropriateness of the parallel which is drawn, and clearly again bear in mind that this is not the case of a jury and we would not be influenced by the type of the parallel, but why can the witness not say, although it is not a parallel, nonetheless, there was a mixture, as he appears to be saying, in his view of military and political roles, and then he refers to his experience in Kosovo, where he is now; why can he not say that, with his background? Again, it's a matter of opinion, but he's got a basis for saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If that's the view of the Court, Mr. President, that's the view of the Court. But obviously we would be entitled to explore, in some detail, the basis for that opinion, since he professes to be a political expert. And I think that if the Court is inclined to permit him to express his opinions, I'm certainly prepared to go into these matters on cross-examination, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We think that, first of all, it will be for the Prosecution to establish that the witness can give these opinions. We'll hear the evidence about that. In any event, we think that references to Hitler will be extremely unhelpful and should be excised because of the inflammatory nature of that sort of reference. Now, there was a third point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The third point was that the Defence for Mr. Kordic, and I believe I can speak for my colleagues representing Mr. Cerkez, we have no objection to the Prosecution leading this witness through paragraphs 1 to 17 and also, to the extent that the Court deems relevant, paragraphs 40 and 41, which I've just reviewed. That appears to be not contentious. I would also like to inform the Court, with again the permission of my colleagues representing Mr. Cerkez, that they do not propose to cross-examine this witness. Accordingly, I will be conducting all the cross-examination, just so that the Court is aware of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Somers, apart from the matter which is in dispute, which is the background of the witness in order that he should be able to give political opinions, apart from that, you can take it that we've read about his career.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is considered read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can take it that we've read about his career, and there's no need to go into it in any detail. Paragraphs 1 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then start with 17, as I understand. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, apart from the matter which is in issue, which is his political expertise, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That you'll have to cover. Yes. Can we have the witness, please? Can we have the witness? While we're waiting for the witness, there is a matter which I note from last week which I want to raise with you. It concerns the afternoons of the week of the 29th of November. Because of Simic over-running, in which two members of the Court are involved, the afternoons of that week look as though they are going to be required. But before making any such order, I would like to hear from the Prosecution as to what effect that will have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The people dealing with witness arrangements are not present in court at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but we would like to hear from you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Carter, if you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Carter, if I may call you Lieutenant Colonel Carter -- I realise you're retired -- the Chamber has indicated that we may take as read certain points about your background and your training and your education. However, I would like to ask you if you can discuss, from your background, education and training, the times wherein you have had to use the instrument of political analysis and/or military analysis in such a manner that would enable you to analogise contemporary situations and/or leaders, be they political or military, to situations of precedent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. My background is such that for at least 15 years or more, I have had the occasion to rely upon training within the military and subsequently within the United Nations to review documents, records, using various types of information and intelligence in order to analyse and report on that information, whether to -- whether to the Defence Department, the Pentagon, or to the United Nations at various levels, to include the special representatives of the Secretary-General, Mr. Akashi and Mr. Annan, and directly to the Secretary-General's office as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Carter, is one of the tenants of analysis that history is often an indicator of the present or future and thus requires careful analysis and analogy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not invariably, but certainly there are patterns that are established over a period of time. And knowing the background of a particular region or area and constantly working in that area, as I've done in Asia for 16 years and the Balkans for six years continuously, certainly one develops a sense, an instinct, as well as the logic for certain developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have experience, both practical and theoretical and academic, with analysis of structures and figures in both totalitarian and Communist-style regimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By event of my educational background, both in international relations and then in Asian studies, with a speciality in politico-military structures and systems, I learned about Marxist/Leninist doctrine, and then practical applications in Southeast Asia, and certainly in the Balkans in the post-break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your military training, did you have to become familiar with the campaigns and figures of the Second World War, both the Pacific theatre and the European theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, with particular emphasis in Asia. But subsequently, when I was in the military, of course, we were dealing with what was termed at that time the Soviet threat in the Eastern Bloc, its organisation and structure, with emphasis, of course, upon military but also the political over-arching structures that controlled, dominated, the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Has your experience allowed you to compare and analogise the actions, designs, objectives of certain military and political figures from regime to regime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it enables one to, let's say, look at certain patterns or parallels that exist over time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Carter, turning to Bosnia, did you have any observation about the comparison between the weaponry of the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Initially, during my early days in Bosnia, November of 1993, and until the war between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosniaks concluded as of about 1 March 1994, one could see the relative inferiority of the ABiH weaponry in contrast to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you characterise in any way the Bosnian army as one of heavy artillery or in some other capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was mainly light infantry in nature. They would rely upon mass manpower to achieve its goals rather than the use of weaponry, whether it be artillery or armour, although they did possess some limited quantities of armour and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you please explain the terms "internal lines of communication" and how this term relates to HVO superior positioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The HVO benefited from internal lines of communication in that their areas of control within Central Bosnia were small pockets in Kiseljak, Vares, also the Lasva Valley and the Vrbas Valley, and they controlled the main roads through those areas, and so they were able to rapidly move forces from one threatened area to another. Of course, many of these pockets were surrounded by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On how many fronts were you aware of the ABiH having to fight, and did this affect its status of advantage or disadvantage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly the ABiH suffered from the fact that it had no organised army to begin with, had no external means of support or supply, basically, and it had to fight on two fronts simultaneously during much of the war from basically 1992 until early 1994, both against the Serbs and the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You referred both to the Vrbas and Lasva Valleys. Could you indicate which is the principal city of the Vrbas Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The principal city would have been Vitez. That's where the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Of the Vrbas, not the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Vrbas Valley, the principal city would have been Gornji Vakuf/Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is Prozor also in the Vrbas Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. It's on the edge the valley, above the Makljen Ridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the HVO renting artillery or tanks from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my capacity as a civil affairs officer, we certainly had meetings in Sarajevo of all the civil affairs officers, and part of my area of responsibility bordered on Kiseljak, and we had reports from the UNPROFOR forces, the UNMOs, that is, U.N. military observers, and civil affairs officers, that there was an exchange basically between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats, but regarding equipment usage and rental, after a certain point in time during the war. I believe it would have been the fall of '93.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Kiseljak is one of the municipalities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. It bordered on the edge of what at that time was controlled by the Bosnian Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Ivan Santic? Would you describe his position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to ask the witness. We know who he is; he is the mayor of Vitez. I don't think there is any dispute about that. Perhaps you could just deal briefly with the witness's impression of him in relation to the accused Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the course of your numerous dealings with Ivan Santic, did you come to any conclusion about the level of authority which he had, and to whom, if anyone, he was subordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first made contact with Mayor Santic as of mid to late November, 1993; had frequent contacts, not quite daily, but almost, after that. As the mayor, he looked after certain administrative issues within the municipality, but on political issues he deferred to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Although he was a mayor of a municipality or town, did you hear him make comments which could be described as derogatory toward the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he frequently referred to them as "balija," which is a pejorative term for Muslims, and suggested that for air drops, that pork should be air-dropped to the Muslims. This is not a particularly unique prejudice on the part of some of the Bosnian Croats, but he certainly expressed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally hear Dario Kordic make any comment about the Christian world vis-a-vis the Islamic world or its culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to that, Your Honour. It lacks a time period. Could we have some indication of when this exchange occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The first time that I would have heard something of that nature would have been in a meeting at the Wolf's Lair; I believe it was February of '94, then and subsequently on a couple of occasions in -- later in '94, in the summer, and even in '95, he believed that Bosnian Croats -- for that matter, Croatians -- had a historic duty to defend Christendom against inferior Muslim culture.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the nature of the authority or responsibility for the HVO throughout HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO had a security role, and of course during times of conflict, its presence and authority reached into almost every aspect of society, to include the delivery of humanitarian aid, the exchange of prisoners and bodies, the distribution of food, water, electricity. And certainly in the political sphere, there was a blurring of roles between that of the HVO and the party itself, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was, then, military intervention and involvement in traditionally civilian aspects of life the norm, or was it an aberration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the norm. This is a pattern that manifested itself in Bosnia, and I saw it in Croatia as well, and in Serbia, and presently I'm witnessing it in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had indicated certain areas that were falling under that control. What is your observation as to the use of these areas or resources as instruments of warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't ascribe it to any one particular side. Both sides used water and electricity, the distribution, the delivery of food, humanitarian aid, or the exchange of bodies, prisoners, and wounded, in a political fashion. Although the Bosnian Croats denied that they did such, in fact they did do -- they did manipulate these for political purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What particular forces of government within political or military leadership become blurred, as you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the HVO -- the roles of the HVO and the party, the HDZ, tended to become more blurred and the more operational and tactical down on the level. Certainly at the Bosnia-wide level there was a blending, but less so. But at the operational level, let's say the operational zones, whether they were southeast, northwest, central zone, or the Posavina zone, the identity of the individual, the political party leader, tended to become also the primary HVO leader. In other words, in military parlance, "Clausewitz on War" stated that war is an extension of politics by other means. Mao says that power grows out of the barrel of a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure this is right, but I think, Colonel, we would be most helped if you would restrict your evidence to what you saw in Bosnia. That would be of real assistance to us, as opposed to the more general historical background, if you could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- distinguish between those two strands, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was merely pointing out that there is a theoretical blending which becomes practical in nature on the ground in Bosnia, where the political party rules over the military execution of tactical events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it your observation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, for Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's put that in a less leading fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry; I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's just as well. Tell us about Mr. Kordic and his role, as you observed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I wouldn't want to overdraw the analogy and certainly not infer that the personages are of the same ilk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me; may I just stop you for a moment. You were not in the courtroom earlier, but I would ask that any particular figure may not be named, historical figure, but perhaps a political regime analogy if you wish, but I would be cautious, and the Court has cautioned us not to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you are looking for a World War II analogy, it would be the identification of the National Socialist Party and the Wehrmacht being directed by that party. A similar sort of thing, but at a much lower level, at the operational zone central in Bosnia. Basically the individual within the old Soviet system, although there is a carryover which still continues to this day in Croatia, Bosnia, and Kosovo, and Belgrade, of course, that the political zampolit or political officer ensures that political direction is executed down through the military chain at the ground level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, could you please ask the witness if that is not the case the world over, when the military serve a particular policy; but military are not part of the politics; they are applied, but doesn't it happen in all the systems in the world, democratic or the military ones which follow a certain political line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To an extent, yes, sir; but in democracies, there is a distinction between the political party, per se, in this case the HDZ, whereas -- let's take the United States, which I'm probably more equipped to discuss. It's no particular political party; in fact, it's the government that develops the policy, not the party that develops the policy. And there is not the blending in the field at the military level, let's say the corps, division, brigade level, where you have a political officer overseeing execution of military events on the ground. If I could elaborate a little bit also, within the old stream system in Yugoslavia, which still continues to a degree, the Ministry of Defence would look over main-line conventional units; in the case of the HVO, let's say, the 110, the 111 Brigade up in the north, whereas the Ministry of Interior would tend to look after the police, special police, and the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which leads to your observations on the nature of the police in societies and republics of the former Yugoslavia. Can you comment about the use of the police: Is it as traditionally in the west, or does it have another type of use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In former Yugoslavia, whether it be during the initial breakup, in which the Serb special police used their tactics in order to agitate, or in the case of in Bosnia, where the Bosnian Croats tended to use special police in order to agitate, to force out the movement of people through the use of propaganda or outright intimidation in order to bring about certain developments, whether it be the forced raising of a flag, or lowering of a flag, or integration of Muslim conscripts into the HVO rather than having them independent; things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know from experience whether or not the use of the police is restricted just toward the military, or does it also serve as an instrument of the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact it tends to be used more as an instrument of the political leadership, which controls both the military and the police, whereas the military leaders, let's say in the case of General Blaskic, would have been most likely confined to only using conventional main-line units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My colleagues have brought to my attention that in the course of asking one question, I did not get a complete answer, and I wonder if the Court would indulge me: On the issue of comments, derogatory comments by Mr. Kordic toward the Muslim population, do you recall any comment about the cultural level of the Muslim population that was made by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I believe I did address that earlier when I mentioned that they had a historic duty to defend Christendom against culturally inferior Muslim culture.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The White Road Convoy in 1993, in December, what distinguished it from other convoys? Was it a U.N. Convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the convoy was put together by the efforts of Dr. Slobodan Lang, a Croatian from the republic of Croatia, and also some Muslim imams, and the Bosniak representatives, to provide aid into Central Bosnia. There were some 200 trucks, with distribution to go equally to both nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Meaning Muslim and Croat, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you indicate the routes by which the trucks were to come from Croatia down to their destinations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went from Zagreb to Split and then up to Tomislavgrad via Route Triangle and Diamond, which was an old logging route improved by the British Battalion, then up to Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje and then Novi Travnik. And then the convoy split at the T-junction, with part of it going to Travnik, that part destined for the Muslims, and then up a back mountain road to Zenica. The part of the convoy destined for the Bosnian Croats went on to Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there discussions -- excuse me. Were there discussions involving yourself, Lieutenant Colonel Williams of BritBat, and the Bosnian Croat and Bosnian representatives about the routes, the actual road routes to be taken, and could you describe the discussions and the ultimate result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. There were previous discussions with General Alagic of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, and subsequently there were discussions, I believe on the 15th of December, with Mr. Kordic, General Blaskic, I believe Brigadier Skender, and the chief of police for Vitez, Mr. Rajic. Colonel Williams was there, Larry Hollingworth of the UNHCR, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: By which route did Mr. Alagic request that the food be delivered or supplies be delivered to the Muslim areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He preferred that the main route, the hard-surface macadam route, be used through Vitez to the flyover and then back to Zenica be used so that the trucks wouldn't be stuck along the mountain road during this harsh weather. The roads were particularly muddy and slippery.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute to the witness exhibits already in evidence, Z2612,3, I believe, and Z2781,2, as well, if possible, as Z2612,7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, if you can reference the approximate routes using a combination, if you will, of the maps, to show preferably the roads by which the ABiH representative wanted the delivery, if you are able to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. General Alagic wanted the delivery to go along what is referred to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO, please, on the projector, if you can. Is the Court getting a projection of the map? We aren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. You're kind of on your own here. I don't have that projection, but if you could show the Court, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Alagic preferred that the routing be directed along what's marked here as E761661 [indicates], from the T-junction here, down through Vitez, around to the flyover which leads back to Zenica this way [indicates]. In lieu of that, Mr. Kordic and General Blaskic insisted that this route over the mountain road from Guca Gora be taken to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which in fact -- sorry. And which request prevailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter request prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did BritBat also have a preference for roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The British preferred the Hardball Express, because it would have been much easier for them. Ultimately they had to rescue quite a few of the trucks that went along the back road, the mountain road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The "Hardball Express" meaning the road --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hard surface; sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you describe Dario Kordic's appearance at the time you met him, and also Colonel Blaskic's appearance on that December 15th meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both were dressed in uniform. Colonel Blaskic did have rank insignia; Mr. Kordic did not. Mr. Kordic was wearing -- other than a military uniform, he had a large wooden cross on around his neck.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any observation about who was leading the discussion, or was it fairly equally led?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fairly equally led. But through body language and otherwise, I would suggest that Colonel Blaskic deferred to Mr. Kordic, and in discussions as well to some degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall the reasons that were given by Blaskic and Kordic for not having the convoy travel along the main HVO-controlled road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concern from their point was security, in that they probably did not want to compromise intelligence along the way, although that was an unstated desire, I suspect, their concern being that they were not too sure that they could control perhaps reactions of the local Croatian populous.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you and Lieutenant Colonel Williams -- sorry. Did you find that a plausible position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not entirely. We found that through experience, that generally when an order was given, that it was pretty much obeyed by the units on the ground. The degree of control and discipline was better in the HVO than it was, say, in the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any incidents of attack by the HVO on the convoy in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, or define the term "interlink" in terms of operational strategy when discussing policy and policy formulation and implementation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the things that we were trained, both in the military and then certainly used during my time in the United Nations, was the use of linkage analysis to determine the degree of command and control through the political levels down to the military levels as far as execution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Concerning Bosnian Croat power and authority and Dario Kordic, did you have any observations that fit into the framework of what you have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that at the operational level for the Central Operations Zone, that the synthesis of both the political and the military existed in the personage of Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How would that affect the planning of policy and its implementation, if you're able to comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been his responsibility to ensure that policies that he assisted in the formulation of that might have been sent from Zagreb, certainly delivered from Grude, Mostar, the leadership there, would be executed in terms of their military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 7th of February, 1994, a meeting was held in the Hotel Vitez between yourself, Lieutenant Colonel Williams, Kordic, and Colonel Blaskic. Could you describe the purpose of that meeting and any particular points which stick in your mind about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, the basic purpose was to discuss the delivery of humanitarian aid and also the exchange of wounded from various areas. In particular, I believe there were some wounded that were in Stari Vitez that required -- that is a Muslim pocket inside the Croat pocket. They required evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall how Kordic and Colonel Blaskic were dressed? And as to Colonel Blaskic, was there any observation about the consistent type of dress he wore throughout your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was dressed in camouflage. I don't believe Mr. Kordic was at that particular time. Colonel Blaskic later, rather than wearing a camouflage uniform, came to dress in a black uniform, black coveralls. And if I recall correctly, basically that was a pattern after the Washington Accords of March of '94.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What are political polemics, as you know the term, and did they apply to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, during any meeting that one might attend, whether it be with the Bosniaks or the Bosnian Croats, they would engage in a little history lesson as to who was guilty for what and attempt to sway the listener to believe their particular line, thus using political polemics to propagandise their particular side. Mr. Kordic, as others, engaged in this practice and at this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At this particular meeting, what was the nature of the accusation about the use of humanitarian matters or aid by one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he accused the Bosniaks of manipulating humanitarian aid and the delivery of water. In part, he was correct, in that the Bosniaks would cut off water from the mountains up above Novi Travnik and not let a complete flow of water through. He inferred that and stated that Bosnian Croats would never do such. However, in fact, the delivery of humanitarian aid, electricity, and water was manipulated by the Bosnian Croat side as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was such a comment referred to, such delivery of water, referred to by Mr. Kordic, vis-a-vis the Muslims, in any part of the Lasva Valley at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to Novi Travnik. But he also said that unless they allowed water to go through, then he would not release or allow the wounded in Stari Vitez and other humanitarian cases to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 21st of February, 1994, a meeting was held at a place called the Wolf's Lair. Would you take whichever map at your disposal would best assist you in showing the Court -- there's a map also in front of you, if you can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may take a second here to locate it. The Wolf's Lair was located down after the T-junction from Busovaca, and generally, although I don't have the grid coordinate, it would have been in this area here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a location called Tisovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's approximately in the same location. Colonel Williams was leading the convoy, and so I wasn't following the map Q Who was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, myself, Larry Hollingworth, Tihomir Blaskic, Dario Kordic, and I think Rajic was there, Anto Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that the chief of police of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was Nikica Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a liaison officer between the Bosnian Croats and the International Community, as well as with the Bosniaks themselves. He tended to inter-relate with a Bosniak by the name of Beba Salko, who was his counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of Brigadier Skender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my understanding that Brigadier Skender controlled the Operational Zone Northwest, which I believe was headquartered out of the Prozor area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Skender, Petrovic and Rajic then also -- sorry. Was Rajic, Skender and Petrovic also at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might refer back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Surely. Or was this also about humanitarian aid and about inspections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It had to deal with the fact that there had been some invasive inspections of UNHCR convoys. And UNHCR, like the United Nations, having diplomatic immunity, was not supposed to be subject to having vehicles physically examined, and the HVO on occasion had stopped some vehicles, opened doors, and had people get out of their vehicles, checked the property, the equipment, in some of these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What assurances were given as to the nature of the future inspections, and who gave those assurances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a protest was basically collectively levied by Lieutenant Colonel Williams, Larry Hollingworth and myself, and after some discussion, Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic agreed that inspections would be limited to visual checks only and not invasive physical searches of the vehicles or the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Kordic make any references to having to seek the approval of the Herceg-Bosna governmental structures or did he make any assurances on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He suggested that normally he would have to have approval, but in this particular case he put the final stamp of approval on that particular policy with regard to the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have anything -- excuse me. Did you participate in any investigation of a massacre alleged by the Bosnian Croats to have taken place in approximately March of 1994 at Krizancevo Selo in the Vitez municipality, and if so, what was checked out and what were the results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had a complaint from Mr. Kordic that there had been a massacre to the north of Vitez at the location of this village. The BritBat troops, the Coldstream Guards, sent a detail up to check it out. They had UNHCR there as well as ICRC and forensic experts, and in checking it out, they did find a grave. But the victims were all victims basically of a conflict, a battle, and not executed or massacred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you find, then, the complaint to be false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a very leading question. If you want to ask it, ask what the finding was. But I think the witness has given the finding. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Washington Agreement or Accords signed at the end of February or the end of March of 1994, were you informed of the presence of -- I'm sorry. Following these agreements, were you informed of the presence of HV or Croatian troops at checkpoints in the area of Divjak in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was an old gas station that used to be located on the left-hand side of the road going to Vitez from Stara Bila, and that was burned down. Just beyond that, there was a small building or restaurant, and it was occupied by HV special police. Both -- the current commander at the time, Lieutenant Colonel Williams, complained about this to Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic, and subsequently there were other incidents in which Colonel Williams' successor, Colonel McCall, also complained of the presence of HV special police in that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the United Nations made aware of the presence of HV troops on the territory of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several instances. When I was personally there, in two different fashions. One, Lieutenant Colonel Williams and the Coldstream Guards actually had to rescue an HV general, I believe brigadier general, and some other officers from the mountainside near Tomislavgrad. They had been stranded in the snow in bad conditions. He had also complained of another incident of the presence of HV troops in Central Bosnia. We, as civil affairs officers, were aware of this in our meetings, when we would hold monthly meetings in Sarajevo. This was reported, of course, in discussions with headquarters in Zagreb. They could come back to us with questions in that regard and ask for information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would the usher please distribute two exhibits, Z1379,1 and Z1380,1. They are at the back of the diary. The two particular exhibits, Your Honours, are Security Council exhibits attached at the very back of the packet which you have just received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention to -- do you have in front of you the document that is from 17 February 1994? This document signed by then Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali makes reference to the presence of HV troops, troops of the Republic of Croatia, on the territory of Bosnia. Are you familiar with the types of allegations set forth in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does this document reflect accurately your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The presence of HV troops in organised military units, as well as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention -- excuse me -- to Exhibit 1380,1, dated 18 February 1994, it is a response fashioned by Mr. Nobilo, Mario Nobilo, the ambassador, the permanent representative, Croatia, of the Security Council to the United Nations. Do you see the explanation, if any, offered for the presence of troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, in paragraph 2, suggests that these were volunteers and that they had departed the Neretva region in Bosnia and had gone south beyond Metkovic, which is basically on the boundary with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the map that you have in front of you, the colour, which is Z2612.7, although it's not a very complete map, if it's complete enough to show the area of Neretva River near Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, basically the Neretva goes in this fashion [indicates] down to Mostar. That's the beginning of the Neretva, and then goes from Mostar down south.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you show the boundary of Croatia and Bosnia, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, not -- well, other than here, [indicates], the southern boundary is not reflected on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet with Dario Kordic after the Washington Accords were signed? Did you have continued contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions. I was requested, through Mr. Kordic's office, to provide security and to be present with him during certain visits in the post-Washington-Accord period so that he could travel freely in Central Bosnia and particularly to Bugojno and Travnik, where minority Croat populations lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Kordic himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, I would like to renew the objection to the testimony beyond the scope of the amended indictment for the reasons previously stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have already ruled on that, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You said "through Mr. Kordic's office." Are you aware of whether or not the request came personally from Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say directly, but I believe it probably did, and also it was relayed to me in addition through Salko Beba from the Bosniak side, because -- well, it's my understanding that they had a fair degree of confidence that if I stated that security would be provided, that it would be provided, and certainly with my personal presence there, that it would add an additional measure of security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In this post-Washington era, did you observe Mr. Kordic have any shift of his public persona, vis-a-vis political or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Rather than being referred to as "Colonel," which he had been on occasion, he took on more of a political public role, and I never saw him again after that dressed in uniform. And then he became, I believe as of April of '94, the vice-president of the HZ-HB or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and then later in the year became the president of the BH-HDZ, the HDZ party of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The security which you arranged for Mr. Kordic, were you aware of any concerns Mr. Kordic had about travelling through Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously by requiring a personal presence, not only mine but BritBat, he must have had some measure of concern for his life and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any particular concerns he had about travelling through territories that were held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Whether he travelled to Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, Travnik, or Bugojno, he feared for his life, as did Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In June of 1994, did you also accompany Mr. Kordic, at his request, to a meeting in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that was a political meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, these meetings were in order to facilitate implementation of the Washington Accords and bring about the federation between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In July of 1994, was a comment made to you by Anto Valenta concerning Zepce, which is part of HZ-HB in the Lasva Valley, and its relationship or connection during the time of the Muslim-Croat conflict which was terminated by the Washington Accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was his contention that there was no connectivity or linkages between those areas as far as direction or chain of command from Vitez/Busovaca, either by the HVO or the HDZ. I knew this not to be true. The BritBat Coldstream Guards' intelligence officer -- not only that one but subsequently the information had been provided that, in fact, there was interconnectivity between those operational pockets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You made a reference to Mr. Kordic's continued authority in the Herceg-Bosna government, which experienced several changes both in name and in form. The HR-HB, from '93, did it assume a different name after the Washington Accords, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the Washington Accords, I believe about April time frame, it then became referred to as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for political purposes, because they couldn't refer to themselves as a republic, per se, and still be within the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That polity had originally been referred to as HZ-HB, the Croatian Community, is that correct, before the change to HR-HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to 1993, that's correct. In 1992, I can't exactly remember, but probably the fall of 1992, early '93.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The former head of the HDZ-BiH, Mate Boban, what became of him if Kordic became the president of the HDZ-BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Boban went to Zagreb, where he assumed the position of director of INA, which is the Republic of Croatia state petroleum and energy company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you change your position within UNPROFOR from civil affairs officer to political officer, and during what time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was civil affairs officer for Central Bosnia Canton basically until January of '95. Then I became the civil affairs coordinator for the entire sector southwest until August of '95, and then went to Zagreb, to the headquarters, to be the political officer for Bosnia-Herzegovina for First Special Representative Akashi, and later for Special Representative Annan, who came in late October through March of '96. He was acting in the dual capacity as the head of the peacekeeping operations and as SRSG. Subsequently to that, I also worked as a political officer with the U.N. liaison office in Zagreb until May of '98, and I continued to follow developments in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would the Court like me to -- I have three more question. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to finish this, please, and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Finishing a question earlier asked about Mate Boban, are you aware of the date of his death and the circumstances surrounding his death in 1997? The reports of his death, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Zagreb at the time, and of course we followed the developments when he was suddenly taken ill and then a ceremony was held. I found it a bit curious, in that it was a closed-casket sort of funeral, and normally for people of, let's say, his distinction, normally it would be an open-casket funeral. But other than that, there's no indications of solid evidence as to his demise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you also serve as a political officer in Belgrade, and if so, when did you terminate your service in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May of 1998, I left Zagreb and began work as a political officer in Belgrade, where I followed developments in the former republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, Montenegro, and in particular, Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a point about your position as legal officer. Did it involve -- perhaps, if you've said this, stop me -- the political analysis of developments in and between Bosnia and Croatia and/or Bosnia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a political officer in Zagreb, yes, I followed developments not only in Bosnia but the interrelationship between the two, particularly with regard to the implementation of the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From 1995 until October of 1997, which was when Kordic was surrendered, did you follow anything about his whereabouts or any of his political career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, I personally saw him in Zagreb. In fact, one case he was attending an affair in Zagreb, and he was known to travel back and forth fairly frequently visiting his residence in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he receive any awards that you know of from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he received some fairly high awards from the Republic of Croatia for his efforts in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a last point, you had kept a diary, copies of the relevant pages of which have been provided to the Office of the Prosecutor and given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would simply ask the usher -- I believe it has been distributed, and I will bring to the Court's attention that it is Exhibit Z2783, and that some of the responses in this testimony came from entries in that diary. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witnesses for the 29th of November, there are two or three, depending on how we do this week, who will have been booked for some time and who are international. One way or another, we'll be able to cope with them. The balance of the week was to be filled with witnesses from the former Yugoslavia. Arrangements have been made for them to attend, but I'm sure that we will be able to cut the list without unusual difficulty, and therefore we are, for that week, flexible. But thank you very much for giving us the opportunity to be heard and to think about it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for being flexible. In fact, having discussed the matter further, I think it likely that two days would be sufficient. So we will have two days remaining -- two afternoons, I should say. Sorry, two afternoons would be sufficient, and therefore we would retain two afternoons in Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So seven sessions as opposed to nine; that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And good morning, sir. My name is Steve Sayers. Together with my colleague Mitko Naumovski, we represent Dario Kordic, and we have some questions for you. I understand, sir, that you have already been interviewed by the Prosecution and by an attorney named Andrew Cayley on August the 23rd of 1996, just over three years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. And at that time you had available the contemporaneous diary that I believe you've brought with you today; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And therefore you are able to consult your diary at your leisure to ensure that the information that you conveyed to that attorney was accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It would have been available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just some matters of background, sir. Your speciality for about 16 years was essentially in matters connected with various countries in Asia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Sixteen out of twenty-five years with the American military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you arrived in the Balkans, I believe, in November of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You first received the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other witness's microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry; could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You received your first briefing at the United Nations headquarters in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How long did it last, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who gave you that briefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, various people. It was an orientation briefing for the overall former Yugoslavia, and more particularly, I think there was a one-day orientation for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, of the one-week briefing that you received, only one day was devoted to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Had you undertaken any study prior to your arrival in Zagreb individually, any individual study to help you understand the political structure that was likely to confront you and the military situation that was likely to confront you when you arrived in Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had started doing some independent reading, one "The Fall of History" -- sorry, "The Fall of Yugoslavia," and the other one a short history of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: "The Fall of Yugoslavia"; that's the book authored by Misha Glenny, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A former journalist; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You also received a briefing from the BritBat component of UNPROFOR -- please forgive the contraction. I believe that the BritBat component of UNPROFOR was the Coldstream Guards regiment when you were present in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was there -- I believe it had arrived sometime in September. I of course arrived in mid-November. It departed in May and was replaced by the Royal Anglians and then by the Royal Highland Fusiliers, and by the Devon and Dorset, all of whom I worked with, and subsequent to that with two -- well, during that time and subsequent, worked with three regimental commanders, Brigadiers Reith, Ridgeway, and Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But it would be fair to say that the Coldstream Guards was the BritBat component of UNPROFOR from the time of your arrival in Central Bosnia until the end of March of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were briefed that Mr. Kordic was the political leader of the Croats in Central Bosnia, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were briefed that Colonel Blaskic was the senior military commander of all of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Of that operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you refer to "that operational zone," is it true that the operational zone formerly known as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone had been renamed, prior to your arrival, the 3rd Operational Zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Colonel Blaskic was the senior military commander in charge of that particular Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative, until he was replaced by Colonel Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Who was the Muslim political leader in the Central Bosnia area when you were there, sir, prior to March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically it was a pretty fragmented situation as far as political leadership was concerned within the Bosniaks. It tended to be almost tribal in nature, oriented around municipalities or villages. Very personality-dependent. I'm trying -- the key political person would have been in Zenica, and Salcinovic would have been the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was that name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salcinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what was his position, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically he assumed the position of governor. During the period of time that he was there, he was one of the political people within Zenica itself. I didn't have -- other than at the municipality level, I didn't have too much contact with the Bosnian leadership at the higher levels -- at that point in time. Later I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your journal, sir, and we have been provided with some relevant pages, the journal was kept contemporaneously; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Now, there is a portion that's missing, which unfortunately I couldn't recover; it's at home in Washington, D.C. It covers a period initially when I was there. It's one of these flip-over notebooks that basically covers daily events from mid-November through to early February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've lost that, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it may be lost. It's packed, and of course most of my possessions are in Washington, D.C., in boxes that I haven't opened for -- well, almost six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Prior to the end of March of 1994, correct me if I'm wrong, but there's only one entry for Mr. -- that mentions Mr. Kordic in your diary, and that's February the 21st of 1994. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: February 21st? Yes, and I believe February the 7th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although that may have been also separately in another -- in another booklet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you mean, another booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because the transition between one book and the other book occurs in early February, and so some notes may have been kept in one and then transferred over to the other, incompletely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, though, that whatever that other book is, you have not been able to consult it or review it in order to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, in November of 1993, you've told us that you were assigned to work as a civil affairs officer in Central Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your predecessors in Vitez were, I believe, first Randy Rhodes; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Randy Rhodes was there I believe from March or April of that year until about September, and then Luc Duchesne took over in a temporary capacity until I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, as civil affairs officer, your principal area of concentration was really the rehabilitation and reconstruction of a country that had been ravaged by civil war; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also we had a political reporting responsibility and interface with political leaders at the lower level, at the municipality level, and of course that inferred some connections with the military as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fundamentally, though, your area of responsibility, if I might use that term, was coterminous with the BritBat area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative. A huge area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Including areas such as Gornji Vakuf in Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and even went down to Tomislavgrad and almost west to Mostar at that point. Later on it did -- in Sector Southwest, it did include that area. And it went north to Zepce, Zavidovici, just to the south of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've given some testimony connected with what you have referred to as Croat pockets, pockets of area controlled by the Croats that you discovered when you arrived in Central Bosnia in November of 1993. Turning to the Vitez/Busovaca pocket to begin with, it's true that that pocket was entirely surrounded by ABiH forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. At one point they were joined, and then -- well, along with the Kiseljak pocket, and then through various attacks, the pockets became divided, but the Vitez/Busovaca pocket basically remained intact and under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Actually, there had been an ABiH offensive against the Vitez/Busovaca pocket in September of 1993, which was unsuccessful, and you were aware of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, you were aware that the ABiH launched another offensive in -- just before Christmas of 1993, on December the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and it's recorded in my journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And finally, the ABiH launched another more successful offensive in January of 1994 which succeeded in -- for a time, anyway -- cutting off the main supply route between Vitez and Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and it forced reliance upon the Santici back road in order to establish any sort of road communications through the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in the Vitez/Busovaca pocket, your perception as a representative of the United Nations was that a siege mentality prevailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the part of virtually everybody, not only in the Croatian pockets, but the Bosniak areas as well, because the Bosniaks were surrounded by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But in the Vitez/Busovaca pocket --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- a siege mentality prevailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect that would be the case, and certainly the Bosniak subpocket in Stari Vitez and Kruscica, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. Wouldn't you agree that this was a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on where you are exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- an extremely complex geographic, political, military and ethnic situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pockets and wheels within wheels and pockets; exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to some of the other pockets, the Kiseljak pocket, you've described; that was also surrounded by ABiH forces throughout the period from your arrival until the end of -- well, up to the signature of the Washington Agreement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. The ABiH controlled the area just outside, to the east of Busovaca, until an area probably, I'd say, five kilometres to the west of Kiseljak. They controlled the road area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you not agree that throughout the first four months of your tour in the area, the HVO was essentially on the defensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In many ways, that's certainly the case, because they had suffered succeeding defeats, and that's one of the reasons that essentially they agreed to the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do not want to spend too much time on this, sir, but there's no question that the following towns were actually captured immediately before your arrival in the area or during your arrival in the area; Travnik for one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Kakanj was before your arrival too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bugojno, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fojnica before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Croat enclave in Vares, the Vares area, which may have been somewhat outside of your area of responsibility, was actually captured in its entirety in November, early November of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I believe it was earlier than that, probably October that that occurred. But yes, that was outside our area. That was basically within the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there's no question that in connection with the military defeats suffered by the HVO in all of these major towns and areas, large quantities of refugees flooded out of those towns following the military actions; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So by the time that you arrived in the area, it would be fair to summarise that the Croat population in Central Bosnia had been squeezed, if you like, into first four and then three enclaves: the Vitez/Busovaca enclave; the Kiseljak enclave; the Vares enclave, which ceased to exist in late October or early November of 1993; and finally the Zepce enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. They had suffered succeeding defeats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, upon your arrival in Kiseljak at the middle -- in the middle or the end of November of 1993, you were confronted by an extremely tense and lawless atmosphere; would you not agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, particularly in Kiseljak. There were a lot of -- there was a lot of random violence and gangs; some military that were engaged in harassing not only citizenry but the U.N. as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Beatings, shootings and robberies were commonplace; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It didn't happen every day, but frequently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you would agree that criminal activity was rampant, and the civil authorities had little, if any, grip on law and order in that enclave, at least as far as you could see; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say, in contrast to the Vitez pocket, that it was more chaotic and under less control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never found anybody from any one of the warring factions who you could ever identify as being in charge of civil affairs in the area, or military affairs, for that matter; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry; again? I'm not quite sure I've caught the direction of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's all right. If I ask you a question which is unclear, please tell me, because that's my fault, not yours. You never were able to identify anybody from either of the warring factions in that area, on the Muslim side or the Croat side, who was in charge civilly or militarily, were you, sir, in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was only there for about a week, and that was in a transition period before going to Central Bosnia, and even during that period, a week or so, I went to Sarajevo for a brief orientation as well. So it really wasn't my -- I hadn't settled into a job, per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one final point in connection with that. While you were there for this one week, Kiseljak was targeted on a number of occasions by ABiH mortars; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
